diagnostic.stem:
A weather station classifies each afternoon by sky condition and wind condition. Its sample space is

$S=\{(\text{clear},\text{calm}),(\text{clear},\text{windy}),(\text{cloudy},\text{calm}),(\text{cloudy},\text{windy})\}$.

The station defines $E=\{(\text{clear},\text{windy}),(\text{cloudy},\text{windy})\}$. Which statement correctly interprets $E$?

options.label: $E$ is the “clear” event; $(\text{clear},\text{windy})$ is an outcome.
$E$ is the full sample space; $(\text{clear},\text{windy})$ is an outcome.
$E$ is a single outcome; $(\text{clear},\text{windy})$ is an event.
$E$ is the “windy” event; $(\text{clear},\text{windy})$ is an outcome.

payload.title: Outcome, sample space, and event: three levels of a weather question
payload.body:
Why do we need these ideas? A weather question can refer either to **one complete possibility** or to **a collection of possibilities**. Probability becomes precise only when we distinguish those two.

Start with three unconditional truths:

1. Before listing possibilities, we choose exactly what features we will record.
2. An **outcome** is one complete result according to that chosen description.
3. The **sample space** is the set of every outcome we are considering.

For example, suppose we record two features: precipitation is **rainy or dry**, and temperature is **cold or warm**. The complete outcomes are

$$S=\{(rainy,cold),(rainy,warm),(dry,cold),(dry,warm)\}.$$

Pause to check the foundation: with those two features, can you see why “rainy” alone is not yet a complete result? It tells us the precipitation but leaves the temperature unresolved. A complete outcome must specify both selected features.

Now we can build the final idea. An **event** is any subset of the sample space—any collection of outcomes grouped by a condition we care about.

The event “rain” contains every complete outcome in which it rains:

$$R=\{(rainy,cold),(rainy,warm)\}.$$

The event “cold” is

$$C=\{(rainy,cold),(dry,cold)\}.$$

The event “rain and cold” is

$$R\cap C=\{(rainy,cold)\}.$$

So the compression is:

- **Outcome:** one complete possibility.
- **Sample space:** all complete possibilities.
- **Event:** whichever of those possibilities satisfy a condition.

Events can overlap: the outcome $(rainy,cold)$ belongs to both the rain event and the cold event. But on a particular day, only one complete outcome occurs.

Whether a label is an outcome or an event depends on what was chosen for the sample space. If we recorded only “rainy or dry,” then “rainy” would identify a complete outcome. When we record both precipitation and temperature, “rainy” describes an event containing two outcomes.

equation.purpose: This captures the definition of an event: an event $E$ is a selection of zero or more outcomes from the sample space $S$.

terms.meaning: The sample space: the set of all complete outcomes under consideration.
An event: the set of outcomes satisfying a condition of interest.
“Is a subset of,” meaning every outcome in $E$ also belongs to $S$.

behavior: Adding outcomes to $E$ makes the event broader.
Removing outcomes from $E$ makes the event narrower.
A one-outcome event is still an event.
The empty set represents an impossible event, while $S$ itself represents the certain event.
assumptions: The features being recorded and their possible values have been fixed.
Each outcome is complete relative to those chosen features.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    Q[Choose what weather features to record] --> S[Sample space: all complete possibilities]
    S --> O[Outcome: one complete possibility]
    S --> E[Event: selected possibilities]
    E --> R[Rain event]
    E --> C[Cold event]
diagram.caption: Outcomes are individual members of the sample space; events are collections drawn from it.

connections: Choosing the recorded weather features determines what counts as a complete outcome.
Collecting every complete outcome produces the sample space.
Selecting outcomes that satisfy a condition produces an event.
Because events are subsets of the same sample space, different events can overlap.

check.stem:
A weather service records each morning by temperature band and visibility:

$S=\{(low,clear),(low,foggy),(high,clear),(high,foggy)\}$.

Let $F$ mean “the morning is foggy.” Why does $F$ represent an event rather than a single outcome?

options.label: It identifies all four members of $S$.

answer.note: Foggy fixes visibility but leaves temperature unspecified. Therefore F contains (low, foggy) and (high, foggy): two complete outcomes from S. An event is a subset of the sample space, while a single outcome specifies both temperature and visibility.

attempt.note: Foggy fixes visibility but leaves temperature unspecified. Therefore F contains (low, foggy) and (high, foggy): two complete outcomes from S. An event is a subset of the sample space, while a single outcome specifies both temperature and visibility.
attempt.explanation: The condition “foggy” matches $(low,foggy)$ and $(high,foggy)$, so $F$ is a set containing two possible results. It does not identify one member because it leaves the temperature band unspecified. It does not identify all four members because the clear cases fail the condition, and it is not empty because two listed cases are foggy.

reasoning.summary: Your reasoning is fully sound: “foggy” constrains visibility but not temperature, so $F=\{(low,foggy),(high,foggy)\}$. You also correctly distinguish an event—a subset of the sample space—from a complete single outcome specifying both recorded features.
